item.title: Video by Left-Wing Group Claims Lindsey Graham Paid Men for Sex
item.description:
A video released on Thursday by a left-wing online news channel features three men who claim that Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died suddenly in July, paid them for sex.

In the 30-minute video released by the Young Turks network, titled “The CLOSETocracy,” one man who identifies himself only by a first name, Kelvin, claims that Mr. Graham paid him for sex when he was 17 and surreptitiously taped him during the encounter.

Another man said he was picked up by a chauffeured car that delivered him to the Mayflower Hotel in Washington, where he said he was paid to have sex and spend the night with Mr. Graham. That man, who is identified in the film as Cory, said he did not realize it was Mr. Graham until months later when he recognized the senator on television during the 2016 presidential race.

A third man said he was paid to have a sexual encounter with Mr. Graham.

Mr. Graham repeatedly denied that he was gay, even as rumors flew about the personal life of a senator who never married. After the release of the video, a spokesman for a conservative group said that Mr. Graham was gay, but dismissed it as an open secret and an attempt to distract voters in South Carolina’s Senate race.

The New York Times has not verified the identities of the men making the claims, or the veracity of their stories. A website promoting the video, called the Lindsey Graham Files, purports to show travel receipts and other documents from the time of the men’s alleged encounters with Mr. Graham.

The man who identifies himself in the video as Cory has also appeared in pornographic productions under the name Sean Harding.

In 2020, he posted online under the name Sean Harding: “There is a homophobic republican senator who is no better than Trump who keeps passing legislation that is damaging to the lgbt and minority communities. Every sex worker I know has been hired by this man. Wondering if enough of us spoke out if that could get him out of office?”

But it was not until after Mr. Graham’s death that he and others in the video went public in naming him and making claims that included allegations that he could not refute and could have resulted in a lawsuit when the senator was alive.

The video release came less than two weeks before the midterm elections, in which Mr. Graham’s sister, Senator Darline Graham, is in a tight race to retain her brother’s seat in South Carolina. Ms. Graham was appointed to finish the remainder of her brother’s term after his death and received President Trump’s endorsement.

A spokesman for Ms. Graham’s campaign declined to comment.

Representative William Timmons, Republican of South Carolina, posted online late Thursday that Mr. Graham was his longtime mentor and friend and that “after 45 years of service to South Carolina and our country, he deserves better than the Left spreading disgraceful lies about a man who is no longer here to defend himself.”

He did not explicitly address the claim that Mr. Graham was gay, but added “the willingness to stoop to homophobic attacks for political gain says far more about them than it ever will about Lindsey.” He said he expected Ms. Graham to win her race by 10 points.

A longtime top aide to Mr. Graham, Kevin Bishop, referred The Times to Mr. Timmons’s post when asked for comment.

Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Republican representative from Georgia who broke with Mr. Trump and left Congress this year, called the men who appeared in the video “brave” for telling “intimate details of their personal lives.”

“The worst kept secret in Washington DC came out today because 3 brave men came out and told the truth,” she wrote online.

“We all knew Lindsey Graham was gay. Everyone did,” Ms. Greene wrote. “So everyone is arguing about how this is old news, why now? Or arguing about being gay, and gay issues.”But the true issue, she added, is “that America’s most powerful leaders keep secrets that comprise them in the most dangerous ways for the security, safety, and prosperity of our nation.”

Cenk Uygur, a co-founder of the Young Turks, promoted his video before its release as a “bombshell documentary” in which he would reveal a Republican senator who used male escorts. But the allegations were greeted with a shrug some on the right, who called discussions of Mr. Graham’s sexuality the worst kept secret in Washington.

“Dear Democrats, This is why we called him Lady Graham,” Andrew Kolvet, a spokesman for Turning Point USA, wrote online, using a moniker that circulated widely on social media in 2020 after Mr. Harding first posted the claim that a Republican senator was paying for sex, who he said had the initials “LG.”

“This isn’t an October surprise, we’ve known this for years,” Mr. Kolvet added. “And blaming his sister for the fact Lindsey was a poorly closeted gay man, is only going to backfire. No one cares.”

Mr. Graham, who died suddenly at age 71 of an aortic dissection, never married, and his single status for decades spurred questions about his sexuality. He was aware of the rumors, but always categorically denied that he was gay.

“I know it’s really gonna upset a lot of gay men — I’m sure hundreds of ’em are gonna be jumping off the Golden Gate Bridge — but I ain’t available,” he said in an interview with The New York Times in 2010. “I ain’t gay. Sorry.”

During his 23 years in the Senate, Mr. Graham, an energetic, omnipresent Washington fixture who condemned Mr. Trump before becoming his top ally in Congress, was a vocal opponent of same-sex marriage. He voted against repealing “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell,” the policy that barred openly gay people from serving in the military. And he opposed adding a provision to the annual defense policy bill to expand the definition of hate crimes to include sexual orientation and gender identity.

Michael Gold and Emily Davies contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Administration Asks Appeals Court to Intervene in California Ballot Suit
item.description:
The Justice Department asked a federal appeals on court Thursday to step in and accelerate a lawsuit against California, where it has sought to compel the state not to tabulate as many as 20,000 mail-in ballots sent to voters it claims are “likely noncitizens.”

The request jumped ahead of a lower court that was still considering the government’s emergency request last week. The government’s moves came as it has gone to extraordinary lengths to scrutinize the midterm elections, ostensibly in search of instances of voter fraud. Related efforts, such as trying to force states to turn over voter rolls and having homeland security agents interview recently naturalized citizens about their voting history, have been blocked in other federal court cases.

In a filing on Thursday, the Trump administration cited the “critical and exigent nature” of its request, and blamed a lower court’s “silence” so far for holding up the lawsuit. It repeated accusations that California was in the processing of sending and counting “vote-by-mail ballots cast by ineligible noncitizens to illegally participate in federal elections.”

The judge presiding over the case, Judge David O. Carter of the Central District of California, had scheduled a hearing next Tuesday to consider the government’s claims.

It was unclear what evidence the Trump administration had relied on, or what federal data or methods had been used to create the list of 20,000 individuals.

In a filing on Monday, the government wrote that the Homeland Security Department had “received what appeared to be the California voter roster for the general election of 2026,” and forwarded it to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to check against its immigration data.

The agency produced a “refined list of individuals” that homeland security officials eventually distilled down to the list of more than 20,000 people, according to the filing.

California election officials have said the data shared by the Trump administration was riddled with omissions and difficult to parse.

Judges in other cases have raised concerns about the reliability of federal immigration data, as applied to screening state voter rolls. Data sets the Trump administration has compiled to help determine a person’s citizenship have repeatedly been found to be out of date or unreliable for establishing citizenship.

item.title: Ocasio-Cortez Says Democrats Should Stand Up for Trans Americans
item.description:
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a progressive Democrat considering a 2028 presidential run, suggested Thursday that she was sorry that some in her party had not more forcefully supported transgender Americans.

Appearing at a town hall-style event in Portland, Maine, with Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in the closely watched Senate race in the state, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez took a question from an audience member who said that “I and a lot of trans people in America feel that we have been abandoned by the Democratic Party.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who nodded as the question was asked, replied that she wanted the audience member to know how “sorry I am that there are people out there that scare so easily after an election.”

Some in the Democratic Party have changed the way they talk about transgender rights since the 2024 presidential election, when Donald J. Trump targeted Kamala Harris with ads declaring: “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.”

Democratic strategists judged the ads to have been highly effective, and some moderate Democrats said after the election that their party should take a harder line against the participation of transgender girls in girls’ sports, joining Republicans on the issue.

This election cycle, a number of Democrats running in battleground races have spoken out against transgender girls playing in girls’ sports, pushing back against a common attack line from Mr. Trump and other Republicans. That approach, in turn, has drawn criticism from other Democrats, who say their party is turning on a vulnerable community.

Polls show voters overwhelmingly agree with Republicans on the issue of transgender athletes’ participation in women’s sports. And some Democrats argue that siding with Republicans on the issue, while downplaying its significance, is politically prudent.

But Ms. Ocasio-Cortez argued in Maine that “the moment you compromise the rights of a trans person in America, you compromise the rights of every citizen in America.”

She tied transgender rights to women’s rights. “I support the rights of trans women because I’m a girl’s girl,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said.

Mr. Jackson, a progressive Democrat who is in a tight race against the Republican senator Susan Collins, nodded along to Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s answer but did not address the question directly.

item.title: Trump Rallies to Shore Up Iowa Senate Race for Ashley Hinson
item.description:
President Trump campaigned in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday, speaking at a rally in one of the state’s reddest enclaves as he tries to elevate turnout for Representative Ashley Hinson in the tight battle for Iowa’s open Senate seat.

As Iowa reels from economic turmoil driven by the war with Iran, Mr. Trump’s tariffs and market volatility, the president centered his speech on red-meat attacks against Democrats, while occasionally touching on Iowa.

The once-purple state had been reliably red since 2016; Mr. Trump has won it three times since. But Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, has led his Republican rival in every major nonpartisan poll this year. Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate nominee, is neck-and-neck in polls against Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee. And only one of the state’s four Republican-held House seats is seen as safe for the party.

Mr. Trump attacked Democrats as communists, accused them of supporting gender-transition surgeries for children and lobbed Islamophobic broadsides against Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, and Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, who is under investigation by Mr. Trump’s Justice Department.

“Ashley Hinson, on the other hand,” Mr. Trump said, “is a mother, a warrior, a patriot, and she will never let far-left maniacs push the radical left insanity on Iowa’s children.”

The rally came just hours after Mr. Trump and Ms. Hinson split on a campaign issue that is dividing the Republican Party less than two weeks before the election.

An attack ad by the Republican candidate for Ohio governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, features the mother of the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton. The ad has drawn bipartisan backlash, in part because Ms. Acton’s mother backed her husband after he was arrested on charges of raping Ms. Acton as a child.

Mr. Trump defended the ad in a social media post earlier on Thursday, urging Mr. Ramaswamy to continue airing it. But hours later, Ms. Hinson called on Mr. Ramaswamy to take it down.

“I think about it as a mom, and you think about childhood, having to relive that trauma,” Hinson told ABC News on Thursday, adding that it is “terrible.” She also called Vice President JD Vance’s support of the ad “ridiculous,” adding later in a post on social media that while she disagrees with him about the ad, she looks forward to “continuing to work with him and President Trump when I’m in the U.S. Senate.”

Mr. Trump again defended the ad Thursday night.

“When I first saw it,” Trump said, “I said, wow, that means Vivek easily will win the race.”

He continued, recounting a conversation with Ramaswamy: “The mother said horrible things about your opponent. Why can’t I have that happen to me? That’s a good thing. But, I said, you’ve got to ride with it.”

It was the latest two-step from Ms. Hinson on Mr. Trump, distancing herself from some of his statements and parts of his agenda, while seeking his support to eke out a win against Mr. Turek, a surprisingly competitive Democratic rival, who has argued that her fealty to the president is hurting her constituents.

Hours before Mr. Trump spoke at the rally on Thursday, Ms. Hinson told the crowd that “I’m not sure that he’s always happy with me when we’re talking, because I ask him for a lot of things for Iowa.”

Mr. Trump also said that Ms. Hinson was always asking him to help Iowa, and to “give a little bit more money to the farmers.”

He continued, “I said, this woman is such a pain. But ultimately, that’s nice, I guess.”

Lawmakers in tough re-election races skipped the rally entirely. Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, among the most vulnerable incumbents in the House, have also broken with Trump in votes on the Iran War.

Mr. Trump again sought to assure voters that the economic pain brought by high oil prices would soon pass. He insisted, as he has for months, that “but one way or the other, it’s going to be done very soon. And your gasoline prices and your oil is going to come tumbling down.”

He also promoted his executive order eliminating restrictions on tax-free, red-dyed diesel and his $8 billion bailout for farmers hurt by high diesel prices. And he reiterated his promise to send each of them $5,000 checks if Republicans retain the House and Senate majorities, drawing cheers. Mr. Trump has repeatedly not followed through on promises of cash payments since returning to office.

Iowa’s economy, which relies heavily on agriculture and trade, has been strained by high diesel prices and tariffs. Republican candidates in the state have seen their margins continually tighten in competitive races as a result of Mr. Trump’s unpopularity.

Asked about Trump’s handling of the economy, his supporters uniformly praised him, saying that President Trump had done the right thing by striking Iran and that short-term pain from tariffs was worth the long-term gain.

“Sometimes you’ve got to have a little hurt to see progress,” said Steve Glackman, 52, a grain elevator manager from Royal, Iowa.
